draft.title: The imaginary unit
card: No real number squares to give a negative answer. So we define a new number i with i² = −1.
Square roots of negative numbers can now be written using i. Split the root: √−9 = √9 × √−1 = 3i.
Powers of i repeat in a cycle of four: i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1. Then i⁵ = i again.

a.why: √−16 = √16 × √−1 = 4i. The option 4 ignores the negative sign, but 4² = 16, not −16.

b.q: What is the value of i³ × i⁴?
b.why: i³ = −i and i⁴ = 1, so the product is −i × 1 = −i. Adding the powers gives i⁷, which is also −i, since i⁷ = i⁴ × i³. Taking i³ as i is a common slip.
b.clue: Write each power as a simple value first, using the cycle of four.

problems.detail: −4i also squares to −16, and the card's own check ((5i)² = −25) invites students to test by squaring. Neither the card nor the why says that √ means the principal root (4i), so a student may wonder why −4i is wrong.

proposal.title: The imaginary unit
card: No real number squares to give a negative answer. So we define a new number i with i² = −1.
Square roots of negative numbers can now be written using i. Split the root: √−9 = √9 × √−1 = 3i. Check: (3i)² = 9 × i² = −9.
Both 3i and −3i square to −9. The √ sign means the root 3i, just as √9 means 3 and not −3.
Powers of i repeat in a cycle of four: i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1. Then i⁵ = i again.

a.why: √−16 = √16 × √−1 = 4i. The option −4i also squares to −16, but the √ sign means the root 4i, just as √16 means 4. The option 4 ignores the negative sign, since 4² = 16, not −16.

b.q: What is the value of i³ × i⁴?
b.why: i³ = −i and i⁴ = 1, so the product is −i × 1 = −i. Adding the powers gives i⁷, which is also −i, since i⁷ = i⁴ × i³. Taking i³ as i is a common slip.
b.clue: Write each power as a simple value first, using the cycle of four.

final.title: The imaginary unit
card: No real number squares to give a negative answer. So we define a new number \(i\) with \(i^{2} = -1\).
Square roots of negative numbers can now be written using \(i\). Split the root: \(\sqrt{-9} = \sqrt{9} \times \sqrt{-1} = 3i\). Check: \((3i)^{2} = 9 \times i^{2} = -9\).
Both \(3i\) and \(-3i\) square to \(-9\). The square root sign means the root \(3i\), just as \(\sqrt{9}\) means 3 and not \(-3\).
Powers of \(i\) repeat in a cycle of four: \(i^{1} = i\), \(i^{2} = -1\), \(i^{3} = -i\), \(i^{4} = 1\). Then \(i^{5} = i\) again.

a.why: \(\sqrt{-16} = \sqrt{16} \times \sqrt{-1} = 4i\). The option \(-4i\) also squares to \(-16\), but the square root sign means the root \(4i\), just as \(\sqrt{16}\) means 4. The option 4 ignores the negative sign, since \(4^{2} = 16\), not \(-16\).

b.q: What is the value of \(i^{3} \times i^{4}\)?
b.why: \(i^{3} = -i\) and \(i^{4} = 1\), so the product is \(-i \times 1 = -i\). Adding the powers gives \(i^{7}\), which is also \(-i\), since \(i^{7} = i^{4} \times i^{3}\). Taking \(i^{3}\) as \(i\) is a common slip.
b.clue: Write each power as a simple value first, using the cycle of four.
